final_answer:
No. The trial court most likely did not err (and mandamus relief would be denied). Under Texas law, a nonlawyer such as a legal assistant who switches sides is subject to a bright-line rule: the employing firm is disqualified unless it took minimal prophylactic measures to protect the former client's confidences. In re Zaidi, No. 24-0245 (Tex. Apr. 10, 2026), is closely on point and appears to mirror these facts. As reported in secondary summaries and search snippets (I could not open the opinion text; see unresolved), it holds that the new firm must admonish/instruct the nonlawyer, at or before the time she begins work on the conflicted matter, not to work on any matter she handled at her prior employment, even if the conflict arises years after hiring, and that late screening after the opposing party raises the issue does not cure the problem. It also reportedly held that e-filing notices showing the assistant's name as filer did not establish waiver as a matter of law, and that a motion filed about two months after discovery was not conclusively an unreasonable delay.

Framework. (1) Under Phoenix Founders v. Marshall, National Medical Enterprises v. Godbey, In re American Home Products, and In re Columbia Valley Healthcare (Tex. 2010), a nonlawyer who worked on a matter for one side and then joins the opposing firm is presumed to have obtained confidential information, and is presumed to share it with the new firm. (2) In re Turner, 542 S.W.3d 553 (Tex. 2017) (as recalled; not fetched) holds that the second presumption is rebuttable by showing that the firm took reasonable measures, and Columbia Valley says it becomes irrebuttable (disqualification required) where the nonlawyer actually works on the same case at the firm's direction, because the firm reasonably should know of the conflict. Disqualification of the firm is required unless the firm shows it instructed the employee not to work on the matter and screened her. (3) Application: Jones had substantial, indisputable access to Apex's confidences on this very litigation (several hundred privileged communications, strategy meetings, litigation documents). Smith Fullingham did not ask about her prior work, never admonished her, and let her work on the same dispute thirteen times over five years and e-file two documents. Screening was announced only after Apex objected in 2023, which comes too late. Her claimed lack of recollection and the firm's assurance that no confidences were shared are not sufficient: the presumption of shared confidences is not rebutted by after-the-fact assertions, and Zaidi reportedly rejects the argument. (4) Waiver: Apex learned of Jones's role in January 2023 and moved in early March 2023, about two months later. Texas waiver-by-delay turns on whether the movant unreasonably delayed after learning of the conflict (Vaughan v. Walther, 875 S.W.2d 690 (Tex. 1994), not fetched). A roughly two-month delay used to investigate and inquire is generally not unreasonable, and Zaidi reportedly treats e-filing notices as evidence, not conclusive proof of knowledge. The prior 2017-2022 e-filings are the best waiver argument but do not show Apex knew Jones's history.

Conclusion: the disqualification order was within the trial court's discretion and should be upheld. Caveats: I verified Zaidi only through search summaries, not the full opinion; confirm holdings and whether there are dissents or rehearing before relying on it.

claims.text: The trial court did not err in disqualifying Smith Fullingham; the order should be upheld.

A firm that hires a side-switching nonlawyer must instruct her not to work on matters from her prior employment, before she works on the conflicted matter; Smith Fullingham never did and screened only after objection, which is too late.
Where the nonlawyer actually works on the same case at the firm's direction, the presumption of shared confidences is conclusive.
Apex did not waive by delay: about two months after discovery, and e-filing notices are not conclusive proof of knowledge.
